issues.issue: The condition that Seller furnish its "most recent available audited" and "most recent subsequent unaudited" statements is expressly "[s]ubject to the last sentence of subparagraph (a)", which allows the other party to decline to proceed at all. Whether a Transaction closed without those statements is void or merely voidable is not stated.

The deemed representation turns on there having been "no material adverse change in Seller's financial condition", a term the Agreement nowhere defines or benchmarks. Because Paragraph 11(vi) makes an incorrect representation an Event of Default, the undefined standard carries default consequences.

The recognition that each Transaction is a "repurchase agreement" and "securities contract" is immediately undercut by its own carve-outs — "except insofar as the type of Securities... or the term of such Transaction would render such definition inapplicable" — so the paragraph both asserts and disclaims the characterization. What it settles for mortgage collateral of long term is exactly what is left open.

The paragraph invokes "Sections 555 and 559 of Title II of the United States Code", a mechanical misdesignation: those liquidation safe-harbour sections are in Title 11, not Title II. The same error recurs and leaves the acknowledged statutory right imprecisely identified.

The qualified-financial-contract acknowledgment operates only "if a party hereto is an 'insured depository institution'", a condition neither Barclays Capital Inc. nor Thornburg satisfies, and is then further qualified by an "except insofar as the type of assets" carve-out. The provision may therefore have no operative content here.

The netting-contract characterization is subject to an exception "insofar as one or both of the parties is not a 'financial institution' as that term is defined in FDICIA", while Annex I Paragraph 5 has each party represent it either is such a financial institution or meets Regulation EE. Whether the Annex I representation forecloses the Paragraph 19(d) exception is unresolved.

Annex I Paragraph 1 makes Annexes III through VII and Schedules III.A and VII.A "a part of this Agreement" and "applicable thereunder", although Schedule III.A is blank ([Insert provisions applicable to relevant country]) and Schedule VII.A lists no Fund or Custodian. Incorporating unfilled annexes also imports Annex VI's and Annex VII's own priority clauses, which override the rest of the Agreement.

Annex I Paragraph 2 says this Annex governs any inconsistency with the Agreement, while Annex VI Paragraph 1 and the Annex VII preamble each declare that they prevail over "any other term of the Agreement" — and Annex I Paragraph 1 makes both part of the Agreement. The instrument therefore has three competing supremacy clauses and no ranking among them.

Annex I Paragraph 3 requires Buyer to transfer Income to Seller on the payment date and forbids applying it under Paragraph 5(ii), but Paragraph 5 of the Agreement relieves Buyer of any such action where it would create a Margin Deficit or where an Event of Default with respect to Seller is continuing. Whether those exceptions survive this Annex I mandate is unresolved.

The right is to substitute "substantially the same Securities", a phrase the Annex never defines and which on mortgage collateral has no self-evident measure; the notice sentence also refers to "such business day" without an antecedent day. What Seller may tender, and when, is left uncertain.

The substitution/termination charge, including "the loss incurred by Buyer directly arising or resulting from such substitution or termination", is to be "solely determined and calculated by Buyer in good faith", with no methodology, source or review mechanism. The only constraint on the number Seller must pay is Buyer's own good faith.

Each party represents it is a FDICIA "financial institution" or a Regulation EE financial-market participant, which sits against Paragraph 19(d) of the Agreement, whose netting characterization is expressly excepted "insofar as one or both of the parties is not a 'financial institution'". The representation and the carve-out cannot both be doing work.

The submission is to "non-exclusive" jurisdiction of Manhattan federal or state courts yet is expressed "solely for the purpose of" enforcement suits, so whether it permits, requires or merely tolerates suit elsewhere is unclear. It also sits unreconciled with any bankruptcy-court forum for the same disputes.

This defines "Business Day" or "business day" only "in relation to any International Transaction", leaving the lower-case "business day" used in Paragraphs 4(c), 11 and elsewhere of the Agreement undefined for domestic Transactions. The Confirmations supply a different, New York banking definition, so which applies to a margin-call deadline is open.

Limb (ii) — any Security "capable of being cleared through a clearing facility outside the United States" — is so broad that ordinary domestic mortgage paper may qualify, sweeping purely domestic trades into Annex III. "[C]apable of being cleared" has no stated boundary or determining party.

Whether a trade is an "International Transaction" — and thus whether Annex III's Prime Rate, Business Day, tax and default provisions displace the Agreement's — turns entirely on the open-ended "International Security" definition immediately above it. The two definitions together make the boundary of Annex III's application contestable.

LIBOR is fixed by reference to "the Reuters Screen LIBO page" for three-month deposits with no fallback if that page is unavailable, whereas the parties' Confirmations use Telerate Page 3750 with a successor-publication mechanism. Which screen rate governs, and what happens when neither publishes, is unaddressed.

The Spot Rate is a quote from "a major money-center bank in the New York interbank market, as agreed by Buyer and Seller", with no fallback if the parties do not agree on a bank. Annex III Paragraph 7 and Paragraph 8(b) nevertheless require a Spot Rate to compute margin and post-default conversions.

For International Transactions "Prime Rate" becomes "LIBOR plus a spread, as may be specified in the Confirmation", but no spread is fixed and none need be specified, leaving the Paragraph 11(h) default-interest floor indeterminate. It also displaces Paragraph 2(m) only for transactions whose international character is itself contestable.

Payment in another currency discharges the obligation only to the extent of Contractual Currency the payee "may, consistent with normal banking procedures, purchase", a standard with no fixed date, rate source or time limit. What counts as discharge is therefore left to be construed after the fact.

The make-whole obligation is switched off where "an Event of Default has occurred and such party is the nondefaulting party", without saying whether the Event of Default must be continuing or must relate to the relevant Transaction. Read with Paragraph 11's continuing-default language, the trigger is imprecise.

The refund of excess Contractual Currency is due "promptly", with no deadline and the same undefined nondefaulting-party carve-out as subparagraph (c). Whether and when a refund was owed is left open.

"[A]ll similar costs with respect to the transfer of Securities" is an unbounded catch-all appended to transfer and stamp taxes, and it allocates them to Seller regardless of which party's dealing caused them. Against Paragraph 11(g)'s allocation of default costs, the overlap is unresolved.

The gross-up excludes any Tax imposed but for a "present or former connection between Payee and the jurisdiction imposing such Tax other than the mere receipt of payment", a connection test with no defined threshold. Whether a given withholding is grossed up therefore turns on an undefined nexus concept.

The obligation is to deliver "any certificate or document reasonably requested by Payor" that would entitle Payee to relief, with no list, deadline or standard for reasonableness. Failure to comply forfeits the gross-up under subparagraph (b)(iv), so the vagueness has consequences.

The notice duty attaches to circumstances "known or reasonably known to it", a phrase that mixes actual and constructive knowledge without defining either. Because breach forfeits gross-up rights under (b)(iv), the knowledge standard matters.

The trigger is a Change of Tax Law that "in the notifying party's reasonable opinion" has or will have a "material adverse effect" on it, with neither materiality nor the reasonableness of the opinion defined or externally testable. One party's opinion thus starts a termination right under subparagraph (c).

The supporting opinion must come from "a suitably qualified adviser", a qualification the Annex leaves entirely undefined and unagreed. Whether an adviser is suitable, and what the opinion must say, is left to argument.

The counter-notice deems the giver to "indemnify the other party against the adverse effect", without quantifying that effect, capping it, or setting a payment mechanism. The indemnity's measure is the same undefined "material adverse effect" from subparagraph (a).

The terminating party indemnifies "reasonable legal and other professional expenses" but the other party "may not claim any sum constituting consequential loss or damage", a term left undefined and hard to line up against Paragraph 11(g)(ii)-(iii) of the Agreement, which allows hedge-unwind and other losses. The boundary between recoverable and barred loss is unfixed.

This adds an Event of Default for failing, "after one business day's notice", to perform any covenant under Annex III, while Paragraph 11 of the Agreement gives no comparable notice-and-cure for its own clause (iii) margin failures. Which regime applies to an obligation appearing in both places is left open.

The nondefaulting party may convert "any currency into a different currency of its choice" and offset across currencies at a Spot Rate that Annex III Paragraph 1 defines only as a quote "as agreed by Buyer and Seller". After a default there will be no such agreement, leaving the conversion rate to the nondefaulting party.

Schedule III.A is incorporated as part of Annex III and, through Annex I Paragraph 1, part of the Agreement, yet its operative content is the blank instruction "[Insert provisions applicable to relevant country]". An incorporated but empty schedule leaves nothing to apply.

Annex IV governs "all transactions" in which a party acts as agent for Principals, while Paragraph 10(ii) of the Agreement has each party represent it will act as principal unless agency is "agreed in writing... in advance of any Transaction". Whether the incorporation of Annex IV by Annex I Paragraph 1 is that advance written agreement is unresolved.

The other party may unwind a Transaction if it "shall determine in its sole discretion that any Principal or Principals identified by Agent are not acceptable to it", an unreviewable standard with no good-faith qualifier. The rescission and restitution consequences that follow are severe and untethered to any objective criterion.

Paragraph 3(b) of Annex IV strips the other party of "a right of setoff in respect of rights or obligations... of Agent arising in other transactions in which Agent is acting as principal", which contradicts the general cross-Transaction setoff granted by Paragraph 12(ii) of the Agreement. Which prevails depends on the unranked supremacy clauses in Annex I Paragraph 2.
